headline: Board approves 44-unit townhouse development at 8 Merrit Parkway and 2-lot subdivision at 66 Concord Street; approves condo conversion at 8 Blue Hill Ave.
summary: The Planning Board approved a conditional use permit and related subdivision actions for 8 Blue Hill Ave, approved a 2-lot subdivision and site plan for 66 Concord Street, and determined it could take jurisdiction over and then approved a 44-unit townhouse site plan at 8 Merrit Parkway despite litigation over a 2024 approval. The Board also approved minutes from September 17, 2026 and found no items of regional impact on the tentative agenda.
decisions: Approved the September 17, 2026 minutes as amended, 5-0-1 with Zoller abstaining.
The subdivision application A26-0160 for 8 Blue Hill Ave was withdrawn.
Took jurisdiction over the conditional use permit and subdivision application for 8 Blue Hill Ave, 6-0.
Approved the Conditional Use Permit A26-0194 for 8 Blue Hill Ave, 6-0.
Took jurisdiction over the subdivision application A26-0167 for 66 Concord Street, 6-0.
Approved waivers for Site Plan A26-0153 (66 Concord St) regarding existing conditions and underground utilities, 6-0.
Approved Site Plan A26-0153 for 66 Concord Street with conditions, 6-0.
Determined that the Fisher vs Dover test was satisfied for the Merrit Parkway application due to changes in state law (HB-631 and HB-1588), 6-0.
Took jurisdiction over the Site Plan application A26-0166 for 8 Merrit Parkway, 6-0.
Approved a waiver for Site Plan A26-0166 (8 Merrit Parkway) regarding existing conditions on adjacent properties, 6-0.
Approved Site Plan A26-0166 for the 44-unit townhouse development at 8 Merrit Parkway with extensive conditions, including a $7,500 corridor account contribution, by roll call vote 6-0.
Determined there are no items of regional impact on the tentative agenda, 6-0.

NASHUA CITY PLANNING BOARD 
October 1, 2026 
 
The regularly scheduled meeting of the Nashua City Planning Board 
was held on October 1, 2026 at 7:00PM in the 3 rd floor auditorium 
in City Hall. 
 
Members Present: Joe MacIntyre, Mayor’s Representative 
 Adam Varley, Vice Chair 
 Dan Hudson, City Engineer 
 Ald. Patricia Klee 
 Larry Hirsch 
 Benjamin Zoller 
   
  
Also Present: Sam Durfee, Planning Manager 
 Connor Muise, Deputy Planning Manager 
 Scott McPhie, Planner I 
  
APPROVAL OF MINUTES 
 
September 17, 2026 
 
MOTION by Mr. MacIntyre to approve the minutes, as amended. 
 
SECONDED by Mr. Hudson 
 
MOTION CARRIED 5-0-1 (Zoller abstained)

- A26-0166, 8 Merrit Parkway

PROCEDURES OF THE MEETING 
 
After the legal notice of each conditional, special use permit, 
site plan or subdivision plan is read by the Chair, the Board will 
determine if that the application is complete and ready for the 
Board to take jurisdiction. The public hearing will begin at which 
time the applicant or representative will be given time to present 
an overview and description of their project. The applicant shall 
speak to whether or not they agree with recommended staff 
stipulations. The Board will then have an opportunity to ask 
questions of the applicant or staff. 
 
The Chair will then ask for testimony from the audience. First 
anyone wishing to speak in opposition or with concern to the plan 
may speak. Please come forward to the microphone, state their name 
and address for the record. This would be the time to ask questions 
they may have regarding the plan. Next public testimony will come 
from anyone wishing to speak in favor of the plan. The applicant 
will then be allowed a rebuttal period at which time they shall 
speak to any issues or concerns raised by prior public testimony. 
 
One public member will then be granted an opportunity to speak to 
those issues brought by the applicant during their rebuttal period. 
The Board will then ask any relevant follow-up questions of the 
applicant if need be. 
 
After this is completed the public hearing will end and the Board 
will resume the public meeting at which time the Board will 
deliberate and vote on the application before us. The Board asks 
that both sides keep their remarks to the subject at hand and try 
not to repeat what has already been said. 
 
Above all, the Board wants to be fair to everyone and make the 
best possible decision based on the testimony presented and all 
applicable approval criteria established in the Nashua Revised 
Ordinances for conditional, special use permits, site plans and 
subdivisions. Thank you for your interest and courteous attention. 
Please turn off your cell phones and pagers at this time. 
 
Per our legal charter, we have a quorum when five members are 
present. There may be some recusals this evening for certain board 
members, but as long as five members are sitting each case can be 
heard. At the discretion of the chair, the order of the cases can 
be rearranged.
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 3 
 
NEW BUSINESS – CONDITIONAL USE PERMITS 
A26-0194  Paul Francis Development Group, LLC (Owner & Applicant) 
requesting a Conditional Use Permit to convert a duplex 
to 2-unit condominium. Property is located at 8 Blue 
Hill Ave. Map E – Lot 216. Zoned A-Urban Residence (R-
A). Ward 4. 
 
NEW BUSINESS – SUBDIVISION PLANS 
A26-0160  Paul Francis Development Group, LLC (Owner & Applicant) 
requesting a 2-unit condominium subdivision through the 
conversion of an existing residential property. Property 
is located at 8 Blue Hill Ave. Map E – Lot 216. Zoned A-
Urban Residence (R-A). Ward 4. (Withdrawn) 
 
MOTION by Mr. MacIntyre that the application is complete and the 
Planning Board is ready to take jurisdiction 
 
SECONDED by Mr. Zoller 
 
MOTION CARRIED 6-0 
 
Connor Walsh, 8 Blue Hill Ave, Nashua NH 
 
Mr. Walsh said he is the property owner. This is a duplex under 
one ownership, he would like to convert that to two condos. He 
doesn’t plan any expansions or changes, he is ready to list it for 
sale. There is no impact to traffic or environmental safety. There 
is a condition regarding individual sewage disposal systems, but 
this is already on city sewer and water. There is no onsite private 
septic.  
 
Mr. Hudson said there is one sewer service shared for the property, 
how will future maintenance be covered? Is there a set of condo 
documents that goes with that? 
 
Mr. Walsh said yes, they have condominium documents drafted. The 
sewer service is considered a commonly owned utility. Each unit 
would be charged 50%.  
 
SPEAKING IN OPPOSITION OR CONCERN 
 
None 
 
SPEAKING IN FAVOR
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 4 
 
None 
 
PUBLIC MEETING 
 
Mr. Varley closed the public hearing and moved into the public 
meeting. He said this seems about as straightforward as it gets. 
He has no concerns. There are no waivers, so it is just a matter 
of conditional permit approval.  
 
MOTION by Mr. MacIntyre to approve New Business – Conditional Use 
Permit A26-0194. The Board finds that the application meets the 
Approval Criteria under §190-133(F). 
 
SECONDED by Ald. Klee 
 
MOTION CARRIED 6-0 
 
NEW BUSINESS – SUBDIVISION PLANS 
A26-0167  Crimson Properties, LLC (Owner & Applicant) requesting 
a 2-lot subdivision. Property is located at 66 Concord 
Street. Map 27 – Lot 66. Zoned B Urban Residence (R-B). 
Ward 3. (Postponed to the October 1st, 2026 meeting by 
Applicant request) 
 
MOTION by Mr. MacIntyre that the application is complete and the 
Planning Board is ready to take jurisdiction 
 
SECONDED by Ald. Klee 
 
MOTION CARRIED 6-0 
 
Paul Chisholm, Civil Engineer, Keach Nordstrom Associates, 5 
Commerce Park N Ste 201, Bedford NH 
  
Mr. Chisholm introduced himself on behalf of the owner. With him 
tonight is Atty. Brad Westgate from Welts, White, & Fontaine, and 
owner Randy Turmel.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the project before the Board is relatively simple 
in concept, but there are a few important nuances to go over given 
the history and location of the property. The applicant is 
proposing to subdivide the subject lot into two parcels, with the 
intent to restore the existing home, raze the carriage house, 
construct a new carriage house in the existing style next to the 
home, and construct a new single-family home with a detached 2-
car garage on the new lot.
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 5 
 
 
Mr. Chisholm said the existing home contains just under 25,000-
sqft of land, with frontages on Concord Street and Hall Ave. It is 
situated in the RB zone and the Historic District. The site is 
relatively flat, contains sandy soils, and city utilities. The 
existing residence is a 5-bedroom single family home, originally 
constructed in 1870. This home is in tough shape, and the 
restoration is underway. There are two curb cuts, one on Concord 
St and one on Hall Ave, and the two connect under a portico. The 
new lot would have frontage on Concord Street and be served by 
city utilities. Both lots will comply with minimum dimensional 
zoning requirements, no variances are required.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said a specific architectural concept has been 
developed based on the existing building envelope and character of 
the surrounding neighborhood. The intent is to draw from the 
surrounding architectural elements that exist around it and the 
streetscape of Concord Street. Both homes will have a detached 
carriage style garage, with an opportunity to house a unit on the 
second floor.  
 
Mr. Chisholm showed renderings of the existing residence and 
proposed new home. The existing home received Historic District 
Commission approval for renovation on July 27, 2026. We have asked 
staff to include the meeting minutes in the packet. This project 
did originally contemplate razing the historic structure and 
subdividing the lot into three new lots, the HDC did not support 
that and the applicant decided to move forward with a two-lot 
subdivision. The new home and carriage house will need Historic 
District Commission approval.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the staff report makes note of two cases that 
came before the Planning Board for subdivision. The first is from 
1987 for 6 Manchester St and 10 French St, Victorian Realty Group 
vs City of Nashua. The second case is from 2008 for 1 Swart St, 
Judith A. Guiterman Revocable Trust vs City of Nashua. The 
materials made available were the court decisions and meeting 
minutes, Atty. Westgate can address questions on the court cases.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the cases do not stand for the proposition that 
subdivision is not allowed on Concord Street, but rather that the 
Planning Board must look to section 190-138 in the Land Use Code 
when evaluating any subdivision. As noted in the Guiterman case, 
these criteria include that the subdivision must be compatible 
with the surrounding character of the neighborhood and preserve
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 6 
 
the future character of the area. The subdivision must be 
consistent with the goals and objectives of the city’s master plan.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said in light of those cases if would like to provide 
some details about the Historic District and the trends and 
elements of this character, and how this proposal has its own 
unique character. He showed an overview of the Historic District, 
which spans a number of different zones from RA to RC and the 
downtown. There’s a broad range of existing uses, including single 
family, multifamily, a variety of commercial uses, schools, and 
churches. There is also significant variation in lot dimensions.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the question is not whether a new lot can be 
created, but how can it be created while fitting into the 
surrounding area. He showed an aerial of the north end of the 
Historic District, from Manchester Street north. Just north of 
Stark Street, we believe there is a transition point between the 
larger lots to the north and the smaller lots to the south.  
 
Mr. Chisholm showed an area of what he considers to be the 
neighborhood of this lot, stylistically. Within this area there 
are about 20-30 parcels. The subject lot is the largest. After the 
subdivision, the remnant parent parcel will remain in the average 
size of about 16,000-sqft, which is typical for lots in this 
neighborhood. The new lot will be a little bit smaller, but it is 
not the smallest in the district.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the blocks to the north and south of this 
property are similar situations that already exist. Lot 65-90 is 
a more narrow, smaller property sandwiched in between two corner 
lots. Lots 66-70 and 66-32 are also a bit narrower and smaller 
lots, each with less frontage than the proposed lot. While this 
proposal introduces a new lot, this pattern is not foreign to this 
section of Concord St.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said taken together with these facts that distinguish 
it from the 1 Swart Street subdivision, this is fully compliant 
with the dimensional requirements. This isn’t a 3-lot subdivision, 
something that tries to maximize the property and squeeze every 
last little thing out of it.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said the existing carriage house was beyond repair 
and it has been razed and will replaced similarly as it had existed 
to the rear of the home.
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 7 
 
Mr. Chisholm said the applicant has developed an architectural 
concept for the new residence that draws on the architectural 
components of the current home. It respects the existing 
development pattern along Concord St while allowing for the 
restoration and productive use of the property. The intent is not 
to introduce something incompatible in form to the neighborhood or 
Historic District, it is to make something compatible while 
reinvigorating a property in desperate need of redevelopment.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said when reviewing a property, the Historic District 
Commission looks at the governing ordinances 190-22(A)(2)(b), 
which deals with the proposal’s compatibility of exterior design, 
arrangement of textures, materials, and the setting. The HDC has 
already approved the applicant’s proposed renovation of the 
existing house and reconstruction of the carriage house. The 
applicant feels comfortable being able to do the same thing in 
replicating that on the new lot as well.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said in terms of abutters, there were a number of 
letters of support. That is a stark difference between the 1987 
and 2009 subdivision cases, those had significant opposition. 
There are two waiver requests, as detailed in the staff report. 
There are full letters addressing those in the packet. We have 
reviewed the staff report and don’t take exception to the 
recommended stipulations of approval.  
 
Mr. Varley asked staff if the Board were to act favorably on this 
application, would the building have to go to the Historic District 
Commission for approval? 
 
Mr. Durfee said correct.  
 
Mr. MacIntyre said the view of the HDC starts a little earlier 
than he said. He is not on the HDC, he is only here to talk about 
the site and subdivision approval criteria. The building is 
historical, it’s from 1898. He’s pleased that they are rehabbing 
that building. One of the criteria is that the plan must be 
consistent with the goals and objectives of the master plan.  
 
Mr. MacIntyre said when he saw the visuals of the proposed 
building, he didn’t see anything else but a 21st century building. 
He doesn’t see anything other than a pitched roof similarity, but 
it’s not a huge diversion from the master plan. He finds it 
unfortunate that this lot will be subdivided because that whole 
frontage area of that street has a lot of big homes that makes 
almost a touring area for people who want to see Nashua
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 8 
 
architecture. When you split that up, you’ve gone against the 
spirit of the geist of that place. But within the context of the 
approval criteria he can’t do anything about it.  
 
Mr. MacIntyre said he read the staff report, and they’re following 
all the criteria of the ordinances and state laws. They have a 
favorable staff report to move ahead. But is there anything he’s 
missing that is debatable for subdividing this land? 
 
Mr. Durfee said he adequately captured it with the comment about 
approval criteria. The scope of this Board is limiting in a way, 
but we have also provided the Board with recent case law that has 
supported past denials of subdivisions within the district. The 
staff report remains neutral on this case; while the proposed lot 
meets dimensional regulations there is quite a bit of nuance here 
with the previous case law. 
 
Mr. MacIntyre said he apologizes for misrepresenting the staff 
report.  
 
Mr. Zoller asked if there are any big trees being removed from the 
lot. That vegetative buffer would be important for the neighbors.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said his client is interested in preserving and 
maintaining as much as possible. There will be some things that 
are just going to have to go. There are two mature trees that exist 
on the adjacent property, they can’t touch those. At the end of 
the day, the folks that do have to judge it are the HDC. That will 
change the shape and form of this. Keeping the trees is part of 
the charm of the property. On the subdivision plan there is an 
easement for sewer service, this section of Concord Street doesn’t 
have any sewer lines. We tried to keep it away from buildings, and 
we will adjust it to save a tree.  
 
Mr. Zoller asked if they engaged with a landscape architect. 
 
Mr. Chisholm said not yet but that is the way to address it. 
 
Mr. Zoller asked what the plan was for plantings, whether to 
enhance the frontage or screen it.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said he’s not a landscape architect but they will 
work with staff to make sure it is appropriate.  
 
Mr. Zoller said there’s a note on the plan for removal of sidewalk 
on Hall Ave, is that for utility work? Will the sidewalk remain?
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 9 
 
 
Mr. Chisholm said correct. The intent here is to make use of the 
existing curb cuts for the driveways. Some areas will have to be 
cut to install utilities.  
 
Mr. Zoller asked if there was any plan to refurbish the sidewalk, 
it is generally in disrepair.  
 
Mr. Chisholm said we hadn’t contemplated it. We received feedback 
from DPW that we haven’t fully digested. It will be patched up in 
areas that’s needed.  
 
Ald. Klee said she is on the HDC, she was there for the first 
presentation but not there for the final approval. The owner made 
some substantial changes from the original plan to raze the home 
and subdivide three lots. He worked with the neighbors. She has 
been in this house and there are some gorgeous elements, but 
there’s not one floor that’s straight. The HDC cannot mandate any 
changes within the building. The owner compromised to two lots 
instead of three. The house that will go in will go under strong 
scrutiny of the HDC, it has to be in keeping of the character of 
the neighborhood. As long as he’s maintained the historic character 
of the Frank Cook home, she doesn’t see this as truly changing the 
character of the neighborhood. She thinks all the rules and 
regulations have been met for the subdivision. 
 
SPEAKING IN OPPOSITION OR CONCERN 
 
None 
 
SPEAKING IN FAVOR 
 
Letter from the following: 
 
Alexandra Libby & Sareth Lork, 40 Courtland St, Nashua NH 
Paul English, 7 Hall Ave, Nashua NH 
 
PUBLIC MEETING 
 
Mr. Varley closed the public hearing and opened the public meeting. 
The HDC will have the opportunity to review the character of the 
building itself. There are some cases, some precedent to consider, 
that the Board could deny this in terms of character of the 
neighborhood. He feels the applicant did a good job of illustrating 
that section of the neighborhood and demonstrated that there are 
a number of other lots that are similarly sized to the new lot
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 10 
 
that would be created here. He would not call the new lot out of 
character with the neighborhood given what we see in the blocks 
north and south of this lot. He is comfortable with the 
determination that this is in the character of the neighborhood.  
 
Ald. Klee said 70 Concord Street is a very old home as well, needs 
a little work. But it has a narrower frontage. If that is in 
keeping with the neighborhood, then this subdivision is as well. 
If this home were farther north she would have concerns about 
having a newer home put in. The HDC members are serious about 
keeping things as historical as possible, so she believes that 
this will be a more modest home. We also allowed a subdivision on 
Manchester St within the Historic District. These two streets are 
very different animals, but it’s something we have already done.  
 
Mr. MacIntyre said it’s not a deal breaker for him, but the 
discussion for him is whether or not they want to make a 
subdivision on this lot, and secondarily whether this aligns with 
the goals and strategies of the master plan. That’s debatable. 
Another one is unique aesthetic, architectural and visual 
character of nearby buildings shall be maintained, and the site 
plan shall be in harmony with the character. This is borderline. 
The Planning Board sometimes has to make tough calls. The guideline 
of staying to the rules and regulations is the real magna carta, 
but there will come a time where you’ll have to make some decisions 
that are not necessarily black and white. In his view there’s some 
grey in here, but the owner is doing what he is allowed to do. He 
hopes the HDC works to keep a good aesthetic on the new house.  
 
Ald. Klee said the proposed location of the building is setback 
even further than 62 Concord St, so it is in keeping within the 
line of that. There’s less frontage to that lot, there is also a 
parking lot alongside that. She considers this house to be the 
start of the true historic district. She doesn’t see this 
subdivision as a big change. The carriage house has already been 
knocked down, this goes more toward that direction. This is her 
ward, she is very with the neighbors. The developer has talked to 
the neighbors, they might not like every part of it, they 
appreciate the changes he has made. She does not feel this is 
changing the character of the neighborhood.  
 
Mr. MacIntyre said no one came in to oppose this application. If 
it was a little more resistance, he may be more willing to oppose 
it, but there isn’t any.
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 11 
 
Mr. Zoller said this new lot is not providing the least amount of 
frontage on Concord St. This is not the worst lot on the block in 
terms of frontage and size.  
 
Mr. Varley said there are two waiver requests, we will have to 
address them first.  
 
Ald. Klee said when you look at the public comment, the first one 
is a request to withdraw their opposition. The neighbors may not 
like it, but they’re not opposed to it and are willing to work 
with the owner. The people in Ward 3 are not shy, they will speak. 
 
MOTION by Mr. Hudson to approve the following waivers for New

As per RSA 674:36(II)(N), RSA 674:44(III)(e), and §190-148(D),

The Board finds that the application meets the Approval Criteria

NCPB

NEW BUSINESS – SITE PLANS 
 
A26-0166  Merrit Place, LLC (Owner & Applicant) requesting site 
plan approval for a 44-unit townhouse development, with 
associated site improvements. Property is located at 8 
Merrit Parkway. Map C – Lot 2544. Zoned Suburban 
Residence / Flexible Use Overlay District (R-30/FUOD). 
Ward 5. (Postponed to the October 1 st, 2026 meeting by 
Applicant request) 
 
Mr. Varley said this case is coming to us under somewhat unique 
procedural posture. He will let staff introduce that and how we 
carry out that process.  
 
Sam Durfee, Planning Manager 
 
Mr. Durfee said this case, or a very similar iteration, came before 
this Board September 5, 2024. The Planning Board approved it, it 
was subsequently appealed by the Superior Court, and it is 
currently under litigation by the Supreme Court. There is a 
principle in land use that is almost like double jeopardy. You 
can’t apply for the same thing twice, unless there is a significant 
change in the request or there is material change in circumstances. 
It’s known as the Fisher vs Dover analysis, a court case set this 
precedent.  
 
Mr. Durfee said there are two prongs. The first is a significant 
change in what the project is. The answer quite obviously is no, 
the 2024 application was 44 townhouses, this one is 44 townhouses. 
It’s a nearly identical layout.  
 
Mr. Durfee said the second prong is a significant change in 
circumstances. There have been three bills that have amended RSA’s 
674:77 and 674:80, which deal with and specifically address the 
relief the applicant was required to seek in 2024. That relief, in 
the city’s interpretation of the law, is no longer required. The 
relief required was for density, maximum story height, relief from 
multifamily prohibition on use, and age-restriction on the units. 
It is the city’s interpretation that because of these changes to 
state law, that relief is not needed, therefore there has been a 
material change in circumstances. That prong of Fisher vs Dover 
would be satisfied. This is also explained in detail in the staff 
report.  
 
Mr. Varley said the Board must make a determination on whether one 
or both of those criteria are met under the Fisher vs Dover
NCPB 
October 1, 2026 
Page 14 
 
analysis. If we determine that they have not been met, then we 
would be precluded from taking jurisdiction on the case. If we 
conclude that one or both have been met, then we can take 
jurisdiction of the case and consider the case.  
 
Mr. Varley said because the Fisher vs Dover explicitly contemplates
